content: Scoop and run, also referred to as scoop and shoot, is an informal term used to describe the practice of rapidly transporting critically ill or injured patients to a medical facility without significant on-scene intervention. This approach is also colloquially known as GTH TTH (Get The Hell To The Hospital), a phrase sometimes employed by emergency medical personnel to avoid alarming the patient. The term is most commonly applied in situations involving severe trauma, such as violent automobile collisions, where first responders recognize that the patient’s survival depends on immediate treatment at an advanced medical facility. In such cases, responders prioritize quickly scooping up the patient and transporting them to the hospital, often bypassing the treatment of relatively minor injuries. The underlying assumption is that field interventions, such as palliative or first aid measures, are unlikely to significantly benefit the patient and that any delay in reaching the hospital could have dire consequences. In the United States, it is standard practice to transport patients to a medical facility as soon as it is safe to do so. This approach contrasts with alternative strategies, such as stay and play, where responders address as many medical issues as possible on-site, or play and run, where some field treatment is provided but transport is expedited when the patient’s stability is deemed more critical than the delay caused by on-scene care. Emergency medical technicians (EMTs) are trained to make early transport decisions during patient care. They must assess the severity of the patient’s condition and determine whether to load and go (prioritizing rapid transport) or stay and play (focusing on field treatment). These decisions are integral to prehospital care strategies and are tailored to optimize patient outcomes based on the specific circumstances of the emergency.
